title: The Two Sons
question: A father says, 'I have two children, and at least one is a boy.' Assuming equal odds, what is the probability both are boys?
choices: 1/2, since the other child is equally either
1/4, since two boys was always unlikely
1/3, because only BB, BG, and GB remain
2/3, because boys are already confirmed
correctAnswer: 1/3, because only BB, BG, and GB remain
correctExplanation: Exactly 1/3. 'At least one boy' eliminates only GG, leaving BB, BG, GB equally likely — one of three is BB. Information prunes cases; count survivors.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 1/3, because only BB, BG, and GB remain. 'At least one boy' kills just the GG case, not the mixed ones. List all four original cases, cross out GG, and BB is one of three survivors.
lessonContent:
Information prunes cases — recount the survivors.
'At least one' eliminates fewer cases than intuition claims.
List all originals before crossing any out.
Order matters in counting: BG and GB are distinct.

title: The Guessing Pass
question: A 10-question true-false quiz needs 6 correct to pass. A student guesses blindly on every question. What is the pass chance?
choices: About 38%, summing the passing combinations
Exactly 1/2, since each answer is fifty-fifty
1/10, since only one score in ten passes
Near zero, since guessing never works
correctAnswer: About 38%, summing the passing combinations
correctExplanation: Correct — 386 of 1,024 possible answer keys pass (210+120+45+10+1 for scores 6–10), about 38%. Blind guessing passes far more often than pride admits.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is about 38%, summing the passing combinations. Fifty-fifty per question doesn't mean fifty-fifty overall: 386 of the 1,024 possible keys reach 6+. Count keys, not questions — combinations decide.
lessonContent:
Per-trial odds never equal whole-test odds.
Count passing keys among all possible keys.
Combinations, not questions, decide batch outcomes.
Guessing outperforms intuition more often than admitted.

title: The Three Boxes
question: Three boxes hold GG, SS, and GS coins. You open a random box, draw a gold coin, and consider the other coin inside. What is the chance it is also gold?
choices: 1/2, since the GS box is now equally likely
1/3, since two boxes remain possible
Certainty, since silver boxes show silver
2/3, because the draw favors the GG box
correctAnswer: 2/3, because the draw favors the GG box
correctExplanation: Correct — 2/3. Three gold coins could have been drawn (two in GG, one in GS); two of those three leave gold behind. The draw is evidence for which box you hold.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 2/3, because the draw favors the GG box. Count drawable golds, not boxes: GG offers two paths to this observation, GS only one. Observations update which box you're likely holding.
lessonContent:
Count paths to the observation, not containers.
Draws are evidence about which box you hold.
Two-to-one path ratios beat fifty-fifty feelings.
Bertrand's box is Monty Hall's quiet cousin.

title: The Red Streak
question: A fair roulette wheel lands red eight times running. A gambler piles onto black, 'due' at last. What is black's chance on the next spin?
choices: Far above half, since balance is overdue
Exactly the wheel's usual black odds, near 18/37
Zero, since red has momentum now
Certainty, since alternation must resume
correctAnswer: Exactly the wheel's usual black odds, near 18/37
correctExplanation: Yes — wheels have no memory. Eight reds are history, not debt; black pays its usual ~48.6%. Streaks in random data are normal, not corrective.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is exactly the wheel's usual black odds, near 18/37. Independence means history can't load the next spin. Long streaks feel meaningful but occur routinely — casinos price this fallacy into the carpet.
lessonContent:
Independent trials carry no memory or debt.
Streaks are routine output of randomness.
'Due' is the costliest word in gambling.
The wheel's odds reset every single spin.

title: The Waiting Pattern
question: Flipping a fair coin, which pattern typically appears first: HH (two heads running) or HT (head then tail)?
choices: HT, since it can overlap itself into existence
HH, since heads attract heads
They tie exactly, both being 1/4 per pair
Neither ever reliably precedes
correctAnswer: HT, since it can overlap itself into existence
correctExplanation: Right — HT wins the race on average (about 4 flips versus about 6). A failed HH attempt (ending in T) restarts from zero, while HT's fragments recycle. Overlap structure sets waiting times.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is HT, since it can overlap itself into existence. Equal per-trial odds don't mean equal waiting times: sequences overlap differently. After a lone H, a T completes HT but merely continues HH's wait — structure, not luck.
lessonContent:
Equal odds per trial, unequal waiting times.
Overlap structure governs pattern races.
Failed attempts recycle differently per pattern.
'Feels the same' is not 'arrives the same'.

title: The Dice Duel
question: Rolling three dice, a total of 9 beats 10 in folk wisdom. Counting the 216 outcomes shows one total genuinely leads. Which one, and why?
choices: 9, since smaller totals cluster naturally
They tie, by symmetry of the dice
Neither — totals can't be compared
10, with 27 combinations against 9's 25
correctAnswer: 10, with 27 combinations against 9's 25
correctExplanation: Correct — 10 has 27 paths, 9 only 25. Galileo settled a duke's gambling dispute this way: partitions of a total aren't equally numerous. Count compositions, not vibes.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 10, with 27 combinations against 9's 25. Folk wisdom counted partitions (ways to split) instead of compositions (ordered outcomes). Ordered dice distinguish 1-2-6 from 6-2-1 — and the totals differ.
lessonContent:
Partitions differ from compositions — order counts.
Folk wisdom often counts the wrong units.
216 outcomes is a countable universe; count it.
Dukes and Galileos settled bets by enumeration.

title: The Chevalier's Dice
question: A 17th-century gambler preferred betting on at least one six in 4 die rolls, but lost on double-six in 24 rolls of two dice. What explains the reversal?
choices: Dice remember past games and punish greed
The two bets only look equivalent but their odds differ
Double sixes are luckier and rarer by design
Gamblers always lose eventually regardless
correctAnswer: The two bets only look equivalent but their odds differ
correctExplanation: Exactly. One six in 4 rolls hits ~51.8%; double-six in 24 rolls lands ~49.1% — straddling even. The 'equivalent' scaling (4:6 vs 24:36) is a mirage; compute, don't proportion.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is that the two bets only look equivalent but their odds differ. Naive scaling suggests equal chances, but compounding differs: 1−(5/6)⁴ ≈ 0.518 versus 1−(35/36)²⁴ ≈ 0.491. Proportional intuition fails compound lotteries.
lessonContent:
Naive scaling fails compound lotteries.
Compute both sides; never proportion across bets.
Straddling even by 1% decides professional fates.
de Méré's losses founded probability theory.

title: The Airport Swab
question: A security test catches 99% of threats but false-alarms on 1% of innocents. Threats are 1 in 10,000 travelers. A flagged traveler is most likely…
choices: A genuine threat, given 99% accuracy
Equally either, since the test is symmetric
An innocent false alarm, swamped by base rates
Unknowable without interrogation first
correctAnswer: An innocent false alarm, swamped by base rates
correctExplanation: Right. Roughly 1 true flag per 100 false ones (1 threat vs ~100 false alarms per 10,000). Accuracy percentages mislead when bases are extreme — always multiply by the base.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is an innocent false alarm, swamped by base rates. 99% accuracy sounds decisive until 9,999 innocents each roll 1% false-alarm dice. Tests screen; base rates judge. Bayes is just this multiplication done honestly.
lessonContent:
Accuracy percentages mislead at extreme base rates.
Multiply sensitivity by the base before believing flags.
Tests screen populations; bases judge individuals.
Rare targets drown in common false alarms.

title: The Sophomore Slump
question: Rookies of the year usually play worse the next season. Fans smell curses and pressure. What is the likelier mechanism?
choices: Regression: an extreme season is usually followed by a merely good one
Award ceremonies drain athletic souls
Seniors conspire against winners
Trophies add measurable physical weight
correctAnswer: Regression: an extreme season is usually followed by a merely good one
correctExplanation: Correct — regression to the mean. Award seasons select for career-best luck plus skill; the luck component rarely repeats. Extremes are followed by typicals, curses unnecessary.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is regression: an extreme season is usually followed by a merely good one. Best-of-career years bundle peak skill with peak luck, and luck doesn't defend titles. Expect the second year to resemble the career, not the peak.
lessonContent:
Extremes bundle skill with unrepeatable luck.
Award filters select peaks, then peaks relax.
Curses are regression wearing a costume.
Predict careers from averages, not trophies.

title: The Million-to-One Match
question: A DNA match with a 1-in-a-million random chance is found by trawling a database of 5 million profiles. What does the match alone establish?
choices: Guilt at a million to one
Nothing whatsoever about anyone
That databases should be abolished
A lead worth investigating, since trawling multiplies chances
correctAnswer: A lead worth investigating, since trawling multiplies chances
correctExplanation: Exactly. Across 5 million profiles, several random matches are expected — the prosecutor's fallacy confuses P(match|innocent) with P(innocent|match). Database size dilutes single-match meaning.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is a lead worth investigating, since trawling multiplies chances. One-in-a-million per comparison times millions of comparisons yields expected hits. Match statistics need the search size attached — without it, they're courtroom confetti.
lessonContent:
Search size dilutes every single match.
P(evidence|innocent) is not P(innocent|evidence).
Trawling manufactures expected coincidences.
Attach the database size to every match claim.

title: The Green Jellybean
question: Scientists test 20 jellybean colors against acne with 5% significance each. Only green 'links' to spots, and headlines erupt. What is the sound conclusion?
choices: Green jellybeans cause acne — publish the warning
Expect about one fluke hit in twenty tests, so replicate first
Ban all jellybeans as a precaution
Statistics disprove dermatology entirely
correctAnswer: Expect about one fluke hit in twenty tests, so replicate first
correctExplanation: Right. Twenty tests at 5% error each virtually guarantee a 'finding' by chance. Headlines report the hit; method counts the tries. Replicate before regulating.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to expect about one fluke hit in twenty tests, so replicate first. Multiple testing manufactures significance the way sieves manufacture gravel. The famous cartoon is a methods lesson: count the tries, not just the hit.
lessonContent:
Count the tries behind every reported hit.
Twenty tests at 5% guarantee carnival findings.
Headlines harvest; replication verifies.
Pre-register or perish by multiplicity.

title: The Missing Holes
question: WWII analysts armored bomber zones showing the fewest bullet holes in returning planes. Survivors' pristine zones marked…
choices: Where enemy aim was worst
Armor that already worked perfectly
Where hits proved fatal, since those planes never returned
Zones gunners had polished clean
correctAnswer: Where hits proved fatal, since those planes never returned
correctExplanation: Correct — survivorship bias. Returning planes display survivable hits; missing holes mark where damaged bombers died. Wald armored the absence, and losses fell.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is where hits proved fatal, since those planes never returned. The dataset was pre-filtered by survival — holes cluster where planes can afford them. Armor the silence, not the noise: absence is data.
lessonContent:
Surviving datasets pre-filter their own lessons.
Absence is data — armor the silence.
Holes mark survivable zones, not vulnerable ones.
Ask who is missing before patching the present.

title: The Heard Head
question: Two fair coins flip. You learn at least one landed heads. What is the chance both are heads?
choices: 1/3, since HH, HT, and TH remain
1/2, since the other coin is fifty-fifty
1/4, since double heads is rare
2/3, since heads dominate
correctAnswer: 1/3, since HH, HT, and TH remain
correctExplanation: Exactly 1/3. 'At least one head' removes only TT, leaving three equally likely cases with HH among them. Coins don't consult each other; cases do the work.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 1/3, since HH, HT, and TH remain. The 'other coin' framing smuggles in a specific coin that was never identified. Unspecified information prunes cases, not coins — enumerate, then count.
lessonContent:
Unspecified news prunes cases, never coins.
'At least one' kills exactly one of four.
The 'other coin' is a mirage without identity.
Enumerate first, intuit second.

title: The Marble Scoop
question: A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue marbles. You draw two without looking or replacing. What is the chance both are red?
choices: 9/25, since each draw is 3/5 red
1/2, since reds outnumber blues
3/5, since the first draw decides
3/10, since draws multiply and deplete
correctAnswer: 3/10, since draws multiply and deplete
correctExplanation: Right: 3/5 × 2/4 = 3/10. Without replacement, the first draw consumes redness — denominators and numerators both shrink. Replacement status changes everything.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 3/10, since draws multiply and deplete. 9/25 assumes replacement (putting redness back); 3/5 answers a different question. Track what each draw removes, not just what it reveals.
lessonContent:
Without replacement, draws consume their own odds.
Shrink numerators and denominators together.
Replacement status is the first question to ask.
Sequential odds multiply; they never merely repeat.

title: The Blind Pair
question: In the dark you grab two socks from 4 black and 6 white. What is the chance they match?
choices: 1/2, since pairs are natural
7/15, counting black pairs plus white pairs
2/5, since black is scarcer
4/5, since white dominates
correctAnswer: 7/15, counting black pairs plus white pairs
correctExplanation: Correct: (4/10×3/9) + (6/10×5/9) = 12/90 + 30/90 = 7/15. Matching sums two separate pair-paths — black-black plus white-white.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 7/15, counting black pairs plus white pairs. Matching is a sum over colors: black pairs (12/90) plus white pairs (30/90). Single-color thinking halves the answer; add both roads.
lessonContent:
Matching sums over every color's pair-path.
Add both roads; single-color thinking halves answers.
Sequential depletion applies within each path.
Break 'match' into its disjoint cases first.

title: The Lucky Numbers
question: Maya always plays her children's birthdays; her friend plays quick-pick randoms. Both hold one ticket each. Whose jackpot odds are better?
choices: Maya's, since meaningful numbers attract luck
The quick-pick's, since randomness is stronger
Equal — the draw ignores how numbers were chosen
Neither, since birthdays exceed 31
correctAnswer: Equal — the draw ignores how numbers were chosen
correctExplanation: Exactly equal. Balls don't read tickets; every combination faces identical odds. (Birthdays do risk sharing jackpots — but winning odds never differ.)
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is equal — the draw ignores how numbers were chosen. Meaning attaches to players, never to balls. One subtlety survives: popular numbers split prizes more often, so randoms keep more when they win.
lessonContent:
Draws ignore ticket biographies completely.
Meaning lives with players, never with balls.
Equal odds can still mean unequal payouts (sharing!).
Choose unpopular numbers to keep more if you win.

title: The Doubling System
question: A gambler doubles losing roulette bets, certain that one win recovers everything. What flaw sinks this martingale?
choices: Table limits and finite bankrolls meet inevitable long streaks
Casinos ban all mathematics at the door
Doubling is illegal in most jurisdictions
Winning too much gets gamblers arrested
correctAnswer: Table limits and finite bankrolls meet inevitable long streaks
correctExplanation: Right. Exponentials outrun wallets: 10 straight losses need 1,024× the base bet, and limits cap recovery. Negative expectation per spin can't be laundered by sizing.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is table limits and finite bankrolls meeting inevitable long streaks. The math needs infinite wealth and no ceiling; reality supplies neither. Bet sizing rearranges risk — it never creates edge.
lessonContent:
Exponentials outrun every wallet eventually.
Sizing rearranges risk; it never creates edge.
Limits and bankrolls are the system's ceiling.
Negative expectation survives all choreography.

title: The Carnival Eleven
question: A carnival charges $5 to roll two dice, paying $20 for totals of 11 or more. What is the player's expected fate per game?
choices: Profit, since 11-or-more feels common
Roughly even money over many plays
Jackpot riches with patience
A steady loss, since 3 winning faces pay below fair odds
correctAnswer: A steady loss, since 3 winning faces pay below fair odds
correctExplanation: Correct. Totals 11–12 cover 3 of 36 faces (2/36 + 1/36) — fair pay would be $60, not $20. Expected value: (3/36×$20) − $5 = −$3.33 per roll. Carnivals price hope, not math.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is a steady loss, since 6 winning faces pay below fair odds. Count: 11 has two paths, 12 has one — 3 of 36 faces. At $20 for a 1-in-12 shot, the game keeps two-thirds of every dollar long-term.
lessonContent:
Count faces before feeling odds.
Fair pay equals the reciprocal of the chance.
Hope is the carnival's highest-margin product.
Expected value settles every game in one line.

title: The Warranty Pitch
question: A $400 appliance offers a $90 three-year warranty; breakdowns in that window hit 12% of units at $250 average repair. What says the math?
choices: Buy it — peace of mind is priceless
Decline: expected repair cost ($30) sits far below $90
Buy two warranties for double safety
Repairs always cost exactly the average
correctAnswer: Decline: expected repair cost ($30) sits far below $90
correctExplanation: Right: 0.12 × $250 = $30 expected cost versus $90 price — a 3× markup funding commissions and profit. Self-insure small risks; reserve insurance for catastrophes.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to decline: expected repair cost ($30) sits far below $90. Warranties are profits wrapped in reassurance — retailers push them because margins, not mercy, set the price. Insure catastrophes, not appliances.
lessonContent:
Expected cost is probability times price — compute it.
Markups fund commissions, not your safety.
Self-insure the small; insure the catastrophic.
'Peace of mind' has a price — check the tag.

title: The Playlist Cluster
question: A music app's true shuffle dealt three same-artist songs in a row, and users cried 'broken!' So the app made shuffles feel fairer. What did engineers sacrifice?
choices: Sound quality and battery life
Artist royalties and licensing
True randomness, since real shuffles cluster naturally
The entire concept of playlists
correctAnswer: True randomness, since real shuffles cluster naturally
correctExplanation: Exactly. Genuine randomness clusters — streaks are its signature — while humans expect unclumpy spread. Spotify-style fixes trade statistical honesty for perceived fairness.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is true randomness, since real shuffles cluster naturally. Random sequences contain runs; 'looks random' means evenly spread, which is non-random. Perceived fairness and statistical fairness are different products.
lessonContent:
Real randomness clusters; expectations don't.
Streaks are randomness's signature, not its failure.
'Looks fair' and 'is fair' are different products.
Clustering illusions drive conspiracy thinking everywhere.

title: The Jury Majority
question: Each juror independently judges correctly 60% of the time. Which verdict is more trustworthy: a unanimous 12–0 or a narrow 7–5?
choices: 12–0, since agreement among fallibles compounds
7–5, since debate sharpens truth
Equal, since jurors are equally skilled
Neither — juries are pure theater
correctAnswer: 12–0, since agreement among fallibles compounds
correctExplanation: Correct — Condorcet's jury logic. Twelve independent 60% signals agreeing is astronomically stronger than a near split. Majorities don't just win; their size testifies.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 12–0, since agreement among fallibles compounds. Independent errors rarely align: unanimity concentrates evidence while 7–5 nearly cancels out. Count the margin, not just the winner.
lessonContent:
Margins testify, not just winners.
Independent errors rarely align by chance.
Unanimity concentrates scattered evidence.
Near splits nearly cancel themselves out.

title: The Dice Duelists
question: Two players race to 6 round-wins at dice, halting at 4–2 when the table collapses. How should the stakes fairly split?
choices: Evenly, since the game never finished
4:2, matching wins already banked
Winner-takes-all to whoever shouts first
By each player's chance of eventually winning (about 15:1)
correctAnswer: By each player's chance of eventually winning (about 15:1)
correctExplanation: Right — Pascal and Fermat's problem of points. The leader needs 2 more wins, the trailer 4; the trailer must sweep four straight (1/16), so the leader takes ~15/16 of futures. Fairness prices unfinished games by continuation odds.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is by each player's chance of eventually winning (about 15:1). Past wins matter only through the remaining paths: the trailer survives only by winning four in a row (1/2)^4 = 1/16. Probability was born settling exactly this bar tab.
lessonContent:
Unfinished games price by continuation odds.
Remaining paths, not banked wins, set fairness.
The problem of points founded probability itself.
Enumerate finishes before splitting anything.

title: The Exact Streak
question: Flipping a fair coin 4 times, which exact sequence is most likely: HHHH, HTHT, or HTTT?
choices: HHHH, since heads run hot
All equal at 1/16 each
HTHT, since it looks properly mixed
HTTT, since tails dominate late
correctAnswer: All equal at 1/16 each
correctExplanation: Exactly equal — every specific 4-flip sequence holds probability (1/2)⁴. 'Looks random' is an aesthetic; the coin writes each script with the same pen.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is all equal at 1/16 each. HHHH feels special and HTHT feels typical, but feelings aren't frequencies: sixteen scripts, one pen, equal ink. Randomness has no favorite handwriting.
lessonContent:
Every exact sequence ties at (1/2)^n.
'Looks random' is aesthetics, not arithmetic.
Representativeness fools pattern-hungry minds.
Count scripts before judging handwriting.

title: The Second Picker
question: Annemarie calls HHT for three flips; then Bernardo, seeing her call, picks THH. Whose pattern arrives first more often?
choices: Annemarie's, since first picks set the pace
Neither — pattern races always tie
Bernardo's — second pickers hold a systematic edge
Both always arrive simultaneously
correctAnswer: Bernardo's — second pickers hold a systematic edge
correctExplanation: Correct — Penney's game. The second chooser can always counter (take the opposite of Annemarie's second symbol, prefixed by her first two): THH beats HHT 2-to-1. Position beats priority in pattern duels.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is Bernardo's — second pickers hold a systematic edge. Penney's game is nontransitive: whatever pattern you name, a counter-pattern wins twice as often. Going second with full information dominates going first.
lessonContent:
Second movers with full information dominate.
Nontransitive games have no best first pick.
Counter-patterns exploit overlap structure.
Position can beat priority — check turn order.

title: The Streak Premium
question: A bettor wagers that at least one run of 5 heads appears in 100 flips. Should you take the other side?
choices: No: such runs are near-certain across 100 flips
Yes — 5-head runs are freak events
Only if the coin is proven biased
Only on alternate Tuesdays
correctAnswer: No: such runs are near-certain across 100 flips
correctExplanation: Right. With ~96 overlapping windows each holding 1/32 odds, the chance of dodging all of them is roughly (31/32)⁹⁶ ≈ 5%. Long sequences make 'rare' runs routine — length manufactures streaks.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is no: such runs are near-certain across 100 flips. Five heads feels freakish once, but 96 overlapping chances convert freaks into fixtures. Length is the streak factory; windows multiply chances.
lessonContent:
Length manufactures streaks from freaks.
Overlapping windows multiply slim chances.
'Rare once' differs from 'rare somewhere'.
Count windows before pricing run-bets.
